x.ASV: For the Chief Musician. Maschil of David; when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, and said unto him, David is come to the house of Ahimelech. Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man? The lovingkindness of God endureth continually.
x.Darby: To the chief Musician: an instruction. Of David; when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, and said unto him, David came to the house of Ahimelech. Why boastest thou thyself in evil, thou mighty man? The loving-kindness ofGod [abideth] continually.
x.KJV: To the chief Musician, Maschil, A Psalm of David, when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, and said unto him, David is come to the house of Ahimelech. Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man? the goodness of God endureth continually.
x.YLT: To the Overseer. --An instruction, by David, in the coming in of Doeg the Edomite, and he declareth to Saul, and saith to him, `David came in unto the house of Ahimelech.' What, boasteth thou in evil, O mighty one? The kindness of God is all the day.

nt: David actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. While Doeg had caused great **harm** by killing all of Yahweh’s priests and their families ([1 Samuel 22:18–19](../1sa/22/18.md)), those were harmless, defenseless people, so this was not the kind of feat that a true **warrior** would **boast** about. If a speaker of your language would not say the opposite of what he meant as a way of showing how he felt about what he was saying, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why do you boast about killing defenseless people as if that made you a great warrior?]

David is using the question form to mock and ridicule Doeg. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not boast about killing defenseless people as if that made you great warrior!]

Here and through verse 5, David addresses Doeg directly, even though he knows Doeg cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to himself and to anyone who hears this song that he feels very strongly about how Doeg killed the priests of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, here and through verse 5 you could translate what David says to Doeg as if he were speaking to other people about him. Alternate translation: [Doeg should not boast about killing defenseless people as if that made him great warrior!]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The covenant faithfulness of God lasts all of the day]

David is using the term **day** to mean “time,” since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The covenant faithfulness of God lasts all the time]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God is always faithful to his covenant]

x.ASV: Thy tongue deviseth very wickedness, Like a sharp razor, working deceitfully.
x.Darby: Thy tongue deviseth mischievous things, like a sharp razor, practising deceit.
x.KJV: Thy tongue deviseth mischiefs; like a sharp razor, working deceitfully.
x.YLT: Mischiefs doth thy tongue devise, Like a sharp razor, working deceit.

nt: The expression **sharpened** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Like a sharp razor] or [Like a razor that someone has sharpened]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **sharpened razor** is dangerous and potentially destructive, so is Doeg’s **tongue**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Like a dangerous sharpened razor] or [Like a dangerously sharp razor]

David is speaking of Doeg’s **tongue** as if it were a living thing that could devise calamities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what you say causes calamities]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **betrayal**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you who have betrayed innocent people to their deaths]

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all words that destroy others]

David is using the term **words** to represent what Doeg says by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to say anything that will destroy other people]

David is using one part of Doeg, his **tongue**, to represent all of him in the act of saying things that betrayed innocent people to their deaths. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you treacherous person]

t: and/ he will tear away/ you
and/ he will root up/ you

x.ASV: God will likewise destroy thee for ever; He will take thee up, and pluck thee out of thy tent, And root thee out of the land of the living. [Selah
x.Darby: God shall likewise destroy thee for ever; he shall take thee away, and pluck thee out of [thy] tent, and root thee out of the land of the living. Selah.
x.KJV: God shall likewise destroy thee for ever, he shall take thee away, and pluck thee out of thy dwelling place, and root thee out of the land of the living. Selah.
x.YLT: Also--God doth break thee down for ever, Taketh thee, and pulleth thee out of the tent, And He hath uprooted thee Out of the land of the living. Selah.

nt: The verbs in this verse are in a form that Hebrew writers could use to express either a statement or a wish. It would be consistent with the usual pattern of an imprecatory psalm (see the introduction to this psalm) for David to express a wish at this point that God would judge and punish this wicked person. However, he may also be making a confident statement about what God will do. The original audience would have heard both nuances. Use the verbal form in your language that seems most suitable. Alternate translation: [May God also tear you down forever! May he take you away and tear you from the tent and uproot you from the land of the living!]

David is speaking of Doeg as if he were actually a building or wall that God would **tear down**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God will also destroy you]

David is describing one event before describing another event that would precede it. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they would happen. Alternate translation: [He will tear you from the tent and take you away]

David is speaking as if Doeg were actually attached to or part of the **tent** in which he lived and as if God would physically **tear** him from the tent. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will remove you from the tent you live in and take you away]

David is speaking as if Doeg were a plant that God would **uproot** from the soil. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and remove you]

David is using the adjective **living** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [from the land of people who are alive]

Here the **land of the living** represents the people who figuratively inhabit that land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from among people who are alive]

x.ASV: The righteous also shall see it, and fear, And shall laugh at him, saying,
x.Darby: The righteous also shall see, and fear, and shall laugh at him, [saying,]
x.KJV: The righteous also shall see, and fear, and shall laugh at him:
x.YLT: And the righteous see, And fear, and laugh at him.

nt: David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [And righteous people]

Since David has been addressing Doeg directly (even though he cannot hear him) to show that he feels strongly about what he did, you may wish to use the pronoun “you” here instead of the pronoun **him**. However, there is poetic effect in the change of pronoun. David describes in the previous verse how God will destroy Doeg, and in this verse it is as if that has already happened, so that Doeg is no longer around to address directly. Use the pronoun that will be most natural and effective in your language.

x.ASV: Lo, this is the man that made not God his strength, But trusted in the abundance of his riches, And strengthened himself in his wickedness.
x.Darby: Behold the man that made notGod his strength, but put confidence in the abundance of his riches, [and] strengthened himself in his avarice.
x.KJV: Lo, this is the man that made not God his strength; but trusted in the abundance of his riches, and strengthened himself in his wickedness.
x.YLT: `Lo, the man who maketh not God his strong place, And trusteth in the abundance of his riches, He is strong in his mischiefs.'

nt: This verse is a direct quotation of the righteous people described in the previous verse. The ULT indicates that by putting this verse inside quotation marks. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could also use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [They will say, “Behold, the man]

These righteous people are using the term **Behold** to focus their listeners’ attention on what they are about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

These people are speaking of Doeg as if he should actually have made God his **refuge**, that is, the place where he could go to be safe from danger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the term “refuge” in [14:6](../014/006.md). Alternate translation: [the man did not depend on God for protection]

The term that the ULT translates as **man** refers to a full-grown male. It is related to the word that the ULT translates as “warrior” in verse 1, and it can refer to a soldier. The people may be using it in a mocking sense, like David did in verse 1. Your language may have a word or phrase that you can use to bring out this sense in your translation. Alternate translation: [the big man]

x.ASV: But as for me, I am like a green olive-tree in the house of God: I trust in the lovingkindness of God for ever and ever.
x.Darby: But as for me, I am like a green olive-tree in the house ofGod: I will confide in the loving-kindness ofGod for ever and ever.
x.KJV: But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God: I trust in the mercy of God for ever and ever.
x.YLT: And I, as a green olive in the house of God, I have trusted in the kindness of God, To the age and for ever,

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as such a **tree** was secure and carefully tended, so God keeps David safe and cares for him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [But I am secure and well cared for, like a green olive tree in the house of God]

David is using the term **green** not to describe the color of this **tree** but to indicate that it is alive. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [like a living olive tree] or [like a thriving olive tree]

David is speaking of God’s sanctuary as if it were actually a **house** in which he lived. He does not mean that the tree to which he is comparing himself is actually within the sanctuary itself. There was probably a courtyard around the tent that David set up for the Box of Yahweh ([2 Samuel 6:17](../2sa/06/17.md)), just as there was a courtyard around the temple that his son Solomon later built on the same site. In such courtyards there were trees that priests planted and tended. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the courtyard of the sanctuary of God]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in all the ways he is faithful to the covenant of]

x.ASV: I will give thee thanks for ever, because thou hast done it; And I will hope in thy name, for it is good, in the presence of thy saints.
x.Darby: I will praise thee for ever, because thou hast done [it]; and I will wait on thy name, before thygodly ones, for it is good.
x.KJV: I will praise thee for ever, because thou hast done it: and I will wait on thy name; for it is good before thy saints.
x.YLT: I thank Thee to the age, because Thou hast done it, And I wait on Thy name for it is good before Thy saints!

nt: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because you have done this, I will praise you forever]

David is using a verbal form that typically describes action completed in the past. While verbal forms are more flexible in poetry, he may be using this form to describe something that is going to happen in the future in order to show that the event will certainly happen. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use the future tense. Alternate translation: [you will do this]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because your name is good before your faithful ones, I will await it]

Here God’s **name** represents his reputation. David means that he will wait for God to confirm his reputation for being just by judging and punishing Doeg. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will wait for you to confirm your reputation]

Here God’s name being **before** his **faithful ones** represents it being where they can see it. In other words, God has shown them that his name is good, that is, that he deserves his good reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you have shown your faithful ones that it is good]

David is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **ones**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your faithful people]
